bodyHtml:
VWAP stands for volume-weighted average price: the average price of everything that traded, where each trade counts in proportion to its size. It sits next to the volume profile as the other main "where is value?" tool. The profile shows you where volume traded; VWAP condenses the same information into one moving line that tells you the average price paid today.

This chapter covers how VWAP is calculated, why execution desks care about it, how anchored VWAP works, and what the standard-deviation bands around it measure. As with everything in this track, VWAP is a measurement. How traders react to it is a practice, not a law.

How VWAP is calculated

For each bar you take a representative price and multiply it by the bar's volume. Add those products up from the start of the session, and divide by the total volume so far. Most platforms use the typical price, (high + low + close) / 3, as the bar's price; Sierra Chart lets you choose the input, and tick-level implementations use every trade's actual price. The formula is:

VWAP = sum(price x volume) / sum(volume)

Because it is cumulative, VWAP reacts strongly early in the session and becomes steadier as volume builds up. By the afternoon, one bar barely moves it. Session VWAP resets at the start of each session, which is why it pairs so well with session profiles (VP-05).

Worked example: VWAP by hand

Five illustrative bars. For each, typical price = (high + low + close) / 3. The last column divides the running total of price x volume by the running total of volume.

BarTypicalVolumePrice x volVWAP so far

35202.259004,682,0255201.30
45201.581,5007,802,3755201.38
55202.922,10010,926,1255201.81

After bar 5 the VWAP is 5,201.81. Notice how bar 2 and bar 5, the two biggest bars, pull the average toward their prices much more than bar 3 does. That is the whole point of volume weighting: a price where 2,100 contracts traded matters more than a price where 900 did.

Why VWAP matters: the execution benchmark

VWAP began as a benchmark for large orders, not as a trading signal. Investopedia describes how institutions use it to judge execution: a buy filled below the day's VWAP was, on average, a cheaper fill than the market got, and a sell filled above it was better. Some execution algorithms aim to trade in proportion to volume through the day precisely so that the fill lands near VWAP.

That is the practical reason traders watch the line. If large participants measure themselves against it, VWAP is a price many of them are aware of, and price being above or below it is a quick read on who is ahead today. Above VWAP, the average buyer today is in profit. Below it, the average buyer is under water. It does not mean price must come back to it.

Standard-deviation bands

Most platforms can draw bands at a set number of standard deviations above and below VWAP. A standard deviation is a measure of spread: here, how far the traded prices have been from the VWAP on average, weighted by volume. Sierra Chart's VWAP study documents exactly this: bands based on the volume-weighted standard deviation, drawn at multipliers you choose. The usual settings are 1 and 2.

Read the bands as a stretch gauge. Inside one deviation, price is trading close to where most of today's volume was done. Out at two deviations, price is a long way from the day's average. Balance-day traders often look for responsive trade near the outer bands; trend-day traders expect price to "walk" a band for hours. Which one you get depends on the day type from VP-04. There is no band that price must respect.

A caution about the numbers: many traders say price stays within two deviations about 95% of the time. That figure comes from the normal distribution in statistics textbooks. Intraday prices are not normally distributed and the bands are built from the same data they measure, so do not treat any percentage as a probability for your market.

Anchored VWAP

Anchored VWAP (AVWAP) is the same calculation started from a bar you choose instead of the session open. TradingView's help page describes it as a VWAP that starts from a user-selected point. Common anchors are a swing high or low, a gap, an earnings or news bar, the start of the week or month, or the first candle of a displacement leg.

The logic is the same as session VWAP, applied to a group of traders you define. An AVWAP from a swing low is the average price paid by everyone who has traded since that low. If price pulls back to it and holds, the average buyer since the low is still at break-even or better. If price breaks below it and builds volume there, that group is now under water on average. Practitioners use the level as dynamic support or resistance on exactly that reasoning.

AVWAP fits Stryker's framework neatly. Anchor it to the start of the displacement leg that broke structure (chapter 08), and you have a line that tracks the average entry of that move. A pullback into a fair value gap or order block (chapter 10, chapter 11) that also meets the AVWAP is two separate methods pointing at the same area.

VWAP and the volume profile together

VWAP and the POC answer related questions differently. The POC is the single busiest price. VWAP is the average of all prices, weighted by volume. On a balanced D-shaped day they tend to sit close together; on a trend day VWAP lags behind price while the POC may jump to a new node. A large gap between them is a sign that the day's volume is lopsided, which tells you something about the day type.

POC

What it measures: The single price with the most volume.

Best use: The anchor of balance; a reference level for the next session.

Value area

What it measures: The range holding 70% of volume.

Best use: Where the market accepted price; edges for responsive trade.

Session VWAP

What it measures: The volume-weighted average price since the open.

Best use: Who is ahead today; a moving fair-value line.

Anchored VWAP

What it measures: The same average from a bar you choose.

Best use: The average entry of a specific move or group of traders.

Deviation bands

What it measures: Spread of traded prices around VWAP.

Best use: How stretched price is compared with today's volume.

Why VWAP settles down during the session

Because VWAP is cumulative, each new bar is a smaller share of everything counted so far. The chart below measures that directly on the illustrative session from earlier.

This has two practical consequences. First, VWAP in the first half hour is a weak reference: one big bar can drag it a long way. Many traders wait until the initial balance has formed (VP-02) before they pay much attention to it. Second, late in the session VWAP barely moves, so price being far from it at 3 p.m. is a real statement about the day, not noise.

Weekly, monthly and multiple anchors

Many platforms also offer VWAP reset weekly or monthly, which is simply an anchored VWAP pinned to the start of the week or month. These act like the composite profiles in VP-05: slower, broader references for context rather than timing.

It is tempting to anchor VWAPs to every swing on the chart. Resist it. Two or three anchors, each tied to an event you can name (the last major swing low, the start of the current leg, a news bar), are readable. Ten are not. When two anchored VWAPs from different events sit at nearly the same price, that level is worth noting, for the same reason a confluence of methods is worth noting anywhere in the course.

Common mistakes

  • Using VWAP on instruments without real volume. On spot FX, VWAP is built from tick volume. See VP-10.
  • Treating the first hour's VWAP as meaningful. Early in the session it is based on little volume and moves a lot.
  • Anchoring to random bars. An anchor needs a reason: a swing, an event, a gap.
  • Quoting band percentages as probabilities. The textbook 68/95 figures assume a normal distribution that intraday prices don't follow.
  • Fading every touch of the outer band. On a trend day price can ride the band all session.

Key takeaways

  • VWAP = sum(price x volume) / sum(volume), accumulated from the session start.
  • It began as an execution benchmark, which is why large participants are aware of it.
  • Deviation bands measure how stretched price is from the day's average.
  • Anchored VWAP starts the average at a bar you choose and tracks that move's average entry.
  • VWAP and POC measure different things; the gap between them says something about the day type.

Practice exercises

  1. Recalculate the worked example with close prices instead of typical prices. How much does the VWAP change?
  2. On five ES sessions, note where price closed relative to VWAP and the 1 and 2 deviation bands, and label each day type.
  3. Anchor a VWAP to the last three clear swing lows on a 15-minute chart. Record each first retest and whether it held.
  4. Compare the session POC and VWAP at the close for ten days. Find the day with the biggest gap and explain it with the profile shape.

Self-check quiz

1. Why does a 2,100-lot bar move VWAP more than a 900-lot bar?

Because VWAP weights each price by its volume, so bigger bars contribute proportionally more.

2. Why is VWAP an execution benchmark?

Institutions compare their average fill with VWAP: buying below it or selling above it means a better-than-average price for the day.

3. What does anchored VWAP measure?

The volume-weighted average price of everything traded since the bar you anchored it to.

4. Why should you not quote "95% within 2 deviations" for intraday prices?

That figure assumes a normal distribution, which intraday prices do not follow.

5. On which day type is fading the outer VWAP band most dangerous?

A trend day, where price can keep walking along the band.

  3. Anchored VWAP - TradingView Help Center
  4. Volume profile indicators: basic concepts - TradingView Help Center
  5. E-mini S&P 500 contract specs - CME Group
